intro.html: Is it the real thing? These ten words answer that question in different ways. Some promise that something is real, lawful or true to its name; others warn that it is fake, made up or a lie.
Real: authentic, bona fide, legitimate, veritable. Fake: spurious, bogus, counterfeit. Made up or untrue: apocryphal (a story that is probably not true), fictitious (invented) and mendacious (lying).

words.def: real and not a copy; true to where it came from
words.ex: The museum made sure the old letter was {authentic} before putting it on display.
words.ctx: Visitors bought plastic copies at the gift shop, but the dinosaur tooth in the glass case was {authentic}: a real fossil dug from the cliffs nearby.
words.etym: From Greek authentikos, “genuine, original,” from authentes, “a master, one who does a thing himself.”

mn.text: Nell’s book is signed by the author himself, right at the bookstore table: a real signature from the real writer. It is {authentic}.

scene.alt: An author signs books at a table while a happy reader holds up her signed copy.

words.def: real; also, made or done in good faith, with no trickery
words.ex: After years of lessons, Theo’s big sister is now a {bona fide} pilot.
words.ctx: The letter looked like a trick, but it was a {bona fide} offer: the company really did want to buy Dev’s invention, and it sent a signed contract to prove it.
words.etym: Latin for “in good faith”: bona (good) + fide (faith).

mn.text: Fido sniffs the two bones: one is plastic, but the other is the real thing, a {bona fide} bone!

scene.alt: A happy dog chooses a real bone over a pink plastic one.

words.def: allowed by law or the rules; also, fair and reasonable
words.ex: Being sick is a {legitimate} reason to miss practice.
words.ctx: The referee ruled that the goal was {legitimate}, since no player had broken a rule, and all the booing from the stands could not change it.
words.etym: From Medieval Latin legitimatus, from Latin legitimus, “lawful,” from lex (law).

mn.cue: LEG-IT: the LEG kick was LEGAL
mn.text: The referee checks the rule book: Kai’s left-leg kick broke no rule. “Legit!” The goal is {legitimate}.

scene.alt: A referee reads the rule book and declares a boy's goal fair while he cheers.

words.def: truly deserving the name; used to stress that a description fits
words.ex: Granny Mae’s garden is a {veritable} jungle of tomatoes, beans and squash.
words.ctx: The surprise party was no small get-together but a {veritable} crowd: more than a hundred neighbors packed the yard and spilled out onto the sidewalk.
words.etym: From French véritable, “true,” from vérité, “truth,” from Latin veritas.
words.note: Veritable stresses that a description fits (a veritable feast). It does not mean “literally”: Granny Mae’s garden is only like a jungle.

mn.text: Nana Lou’s dinner table is piled so high with food that feast is the only word for it: a {veritable} feast!

scene.alt: A grandmother proudly serves a table loaded with food while a teen cheers.

words.def: false, though made to look true or real
words.ex: The ad made {spurious} claims that the cream would make anyone look twenty years younger.
words.ctx: Ivy’s argument sounded convincing at first, but its reasoning was {spurious}: she had picked out three rainy Mondays and claimed that it always rains on Mondays.

mn.cue: SPY-YOUR-ious: a SPY in a fake mustache
mn.text: The spy’s mustache looks real from far away, but up close it is glued on and false. His disguise is {spurious}.

scene.alt: A sneaky spy in a glued-on mustache and sunglasses is caught out by a girl who points at his fake disguise.

words.ex: The {bogus} ticket looked real until the usher held it up to the light.
words.ctx: The email claimed that Nana Lou had won a free cruise, but the prize was {bogus}: there was no cruise, only a request for her bank number.
words.etym: From old American slang of the 1800s, in which bogus meant counterfeit money.

mn.text: Kai sets plastic bugs on the picnic blanket to fool his sister. Lila laughs: the bugs are {bogus}, not real at all.

scene.alt: A boy tries to trick his sister with plastic bugs on a picnic blanket, and she laughs because they are fake.

words.def: made to look real in order to fool people
words.ex: The shopkeeper held the bill up to the light and saw that it was {counterfeit}.
words.ctx: The handbags at the stall carried a famous label, but they were {counterfeit}: the stitching was crooked, and the “leather” peeled off in the first rain.
words.etym: From Old French contrefait, “imitated,” from contrefaire, “to imitate”: contre (against, opposite) + faire (to make).

mn.cue: COUNTER-FEIT: FAKE money on the COUNTER
mn.text: Rex slaps shiny coins on the shop counter, but the clerk looks closely: they are painted wood! The coins are {counterfeit}.

scene.alt: A sneaky man tries to pay with fake coins, but the clerk spots them with a magnifying glass.

words.def: widely told but probably not true
words.ex: The {apocryphal} story says the town’s founder once out-ran a bear.
words.ctx: Every student has heard about the teacher who never gave an A, but the tale is probably {apocryphal}; no one can name the teacher, the school or the year.
words.etym: From apocrypha, old writings whose authors were doubtful, from Greek apokryphos, “hidden away.”
words.note: An apocryphal story is doubtful, not proven false. It is widely repeated, but no one can show that it happened.

mn.text: Grandpa Gus has a pocket full of tall tales: the fish as big as a boat, the bear he out-ran. Fun stories, but probably not true: they are {apocryphal}.

scene.alt: A grandfather spreads his arms wide telling a tall tale by the campfire while two doubtful teens listen.

words.ex: The detective in the mystery lives at a {fictitious} address that no mail carrier could ever find.
words.ctx: Although the town in the novel feels real, it is {fictitious}; the writer invented its streets, its shops and even its two-hundred-year history.
words.etym: From Latin ficticius, “made up, artificial,” from fingere, “to shape, to invent,” the same source as fiction.

mn.text: A friendly dragon in Pip’s storybook flies over the castle. Fun to read about, but the dragon is {fictitious}: made up.

scene.alt: A boy reads a storybook while the friendly dragon from the story seems to fly beside him.

words.ex: The {mendacious} knight told the queen he had slain the dragon, though he had never left the castle.
words.ctx: The witness seemed calm and sure, yet her story proved {mendacious}: the bus she said she took had not run that day, and the shop she named had closed years before.

mn.cue: MEND-acious: he MENDS his story with lies
mn.text: Caught beside the empty pie plate, Jonah mends his story again and again: “A dog ate it! No, a bird!” Every patch is a lie; he is {mendacious}.

scene.alt: A teen with pie crumbs throws up his hands and makes excuses while his mother stands with her hands on her hips.

after.cap: From the real thing to an outright lie.

after.html: Two words people often stretch. An apocryphal story is doubtful, not proven false: it is told and retold, but no one can show that it happened. And veritable stresses that a description fits (a veritable feast, a veritable army of ants); it does not mean that something is literally true.

opts.s: Experts studied the brushstrokes for months before declaring the painting {authentic}, a real work by the old master and not a copy.
opts.why: A real work, not a copy, is authentic.

items.q: True or false: an apocryphal story is one that has been proven false.
items.why: False. An apocryphal story is widely told but doubtful: probably not true, but not proven either way.

items.q: “By noon the kitchen was a veritable oven.” The speaker means the kitchen…
choices: was so hot that oven is the right word for it
was too small to cook in
items.why: Veritable stresses that a description fits. The kitchen was not literally an oven; it was hot enough to deserve the name.

items.q: The people in a novel are fictitious, but the novel is not ______, because no one is trying to fool you. Which word fits?
items.why: Mendacious means lying. A novel is made up (fictitious), but it does not lie, since everyone knows it is a story.

items.q: Bona fide comes from Latin words meaning…
items.why: Bona fide is Latin for “in good faith”: bona (good) + fide (faith). A bona fide offer is real and honest.

items.q: Type the word for money or goods made to look real in order to fool people.
items.why: Counterfeit money is faked on purpose to fool people.
